services.name: Drain Cleaning
services.h1: Drain Cleaning in Cedar Park, TX
services.title: Drains | JPT Cedar Park Plumbing Cedar Park, TX, TX
services.meta: JPT Cedar Park Plumbing clears kitchen, bathroom, and floor drain blockages in Cedar Park, TX, TX, with inspection, cable work, and next-step guidance.
services.blurb: We clear kitchen, bathroom, and floor drain blockages across Cedar Park.

paragraphs: We hear about a kitchen sink that gurgles after the water shuts off, a shower pan that holds water around the drain, or a floor drain that sends a sewer smell into the room. Those signs often start with grease, soap residue, hair, paper, or sediment collecting in a branch line. We trace the fixture and pipe route before choosing a cable, hand auger, or camera check.

We also look for water rising in a second fixture, because a backed-up tub and toilet can point beyond one trap. A slow bathroom sink may have buildup at the stopper and tailpiece, while a laundry standpipe can overflow because the clog sits farther down the drain line. The location of the backup helps us separate a local blockage from a shared branch or main line restriction.

We treat a drain that stops taking water, sends wastewater into another fixture, or releases a sewer odor as work that should not wait. Wastewater can overflow a sink cabinet, shower pan, or floor drain, and a blockage can pack tighter as more grease and debris reach the pipe. A single slow fixture without an overflow can sometimes wait briefly, but it still needs attention before the line closes completely.

sections.heading: Gurgling sinks and sewer odors
paragraphs: We regularly hear “my sink gurgles,” “the shower will not drain,” “water comes up in the tub,” and “the bathroom smells like sewage.” A kitchen sink that drains only after the disposal stops can have grease in the kitchen branch, while a shower that pools around the strainer often holds hair and soap near the trap. Water appearing in a tub when a toilet flushes can signal a blockage farther along the bathroom line, and a sewer odor can come from a dry trap, loose cleanout cap, or restricted drain. Those symptoms can sound alike over the phone, but the pipe location, blockage type, and work needed can lead to different costs.

sections.heading: Drain callout and camera check
paragraphs: We begin the callout by running water at the affected sink, tub, shower, or floor drain and checking which fixture backs up first. We inspect the stopper, strainer, trap, cleanout, and accessible pipe joints, then note the pipe diameter and the water level left in the basin. A visible trap and fixture check often takes fifteen to thirty minutes; a cable run or camera pass takes longer when the blockage sits beyond the nearby cleanout.

We clear reachable buildup with the appropriate cable and test the drain with repeated water flow before we leave the fixture. We can refit a trap washer or cleanout cap if removal exposes a worn seal, but a damaged underground line, buried cleanout, or pipe section requiring excavation needs a separate booking. We explain what the camera or cable found so the next drain step follows the actual pipe route rather than a guess.

sections.heading: Cleanout access and pipe route
paragraphs: A blockage close to a sink trap or accessible cleanout takes different work than one deep in a branch line behind a wall or beneath a slab. Cabinet shelves, stored items, a tight crawlspace, and a cleanout hidden behind a panel all change the time needed to reach the pipe. A floor drain or exterior cleanout that gives direct cable access usually avoids removing a trap or working through a fixture opening.

Pipe material and the debris inside the line also affect the job. Grease can coat a kitchen drain over a long run, roots can enter older underground joints, and broken pipe can stop a cable from passing through the route. If a camera shows a collapsed section, a buried cleanout, or a drain route that needs excavation or approval, we discuss that separate work before it is scheduled.

sections.heading: Fixture and cleanout location
paragraphs: Before calling, we ask you to note which room has the blocked fixture and whether the kitchen sink, shower, tub, laundry standpipe, or floor drain is involved. We also need to know whether water is standing now, whether another fixture backs up when water runs, and whether a sewer smell comes from the drain opening. If you can see a cleanout cap, tell us whether it sits outside, in a garage, under a sink cabinet, or behind an access panel. Clear the cabinet below the affected sink or the area around the floor drain when possible, since that gives us room for the cable and water test. Call JPT Cedar Park Plumbing at (512) 818-1571 before a partial blockage turns into wastewater overflowing from a sink, tub, or floor drain.

services.name: Water Heater Repair
services.h1: Water Heater Repair in Cedar Park, TX
services.title: JPT Cedar Park Plumbing | Cedar Park, TX, TX
services.meta: JPT Cedar Park Plumbing repairs water heaters in Cedar Park, TX, TX. We check leaks, burners, elements, valves, and temperature problems.
services.blurb: We repair water heater leaks, no-hot-water calls, and temperature faults.

paragraphs: A wet patch outside the utility closet and a shower that never warms up both get called water heater trouble, but they point to different work. Water reaching the hallway can come from a tank, temperature-and-pressure relief valve, drain valve, or pipe connection. Cold water at the bathtub can trace back to a burner, heating element, thermostat, gas supply, or electrical circuit.

We repair both the water heater that has stopped heating and the heater that has started releasing water. We check the tank, fittings, supply lines, controls, and nearby floor before deciding whether a repair part can correct the fault. We also serve water heater calls in Cedar Park, Anderson Mill, Brushy Creek, and Jollyville.

A dry tank that simply produces no hot water may allow time for a planned repair, but water collecting around the base or running from a valve should not wait. Continued leakage can damage drywall, flooring, insulation, and the water heater cabinet, while pressure or burner faults can worsen with repeated use.

sections.heading: No hot water or leaking tank
paragraphs: Customers often call about no hot water, lukewarm water that runs out quickly, or a water heater that makes a popping or rumbling sound. An electric heater may have one failed element and still deliver a short burst of warm water, while a gas heater with an ignition or burner problem may deliver none at all.

Water under the tank can come from the temperature-and-pressure relief valve, the drain valve, a union above the heater, or corrosion at the tank seam. A dripping relief valve and a leaking tank can look alike from the floor, even though the repair work differs.

Rust-colored water, a sulfur-like odor at the hot tap, or a pilot light that will not remain lit can also lead back to the heater. Each symptom can involve a separate part and a separate amount of work, so we inspect the source before tying the call to one repair.

sections.heading: Water heater inspection
paragraphs: We start the visit by checking the rating plate, tank exterior, supply connections, shutoff valve, drain valve, and relief discharge pipe. On an electric unit, we check the disconnect, voltage at the terminals, thermostat response, and heating elements. On a gas unit, we inspect the burner compartment, ignition components, vent connection, and flame operation.

Initial testing commonly takes 30 to 60 minutes, depending on access and whether the tank must heat through a cycle. We measure water temperature, check inlet water pressure where needed, and look for moisture around threaded fittings and the tank base. A temperature-and-pressure relief valve normally needs a discharge pipe that terminates close to the floor rather than spraying into the room.

Thermostats, elements, relief valves, drain valves, and accessible connections can often be repaired during the same visit when the correct part is available. A corroded tank, seized shutoff, inaccessible piping, or a part that must be ordered may require a return visit or a separate replacement discussion.

sections.heading: Tank age and shutoff valve
paragraphs: The tank age changes the repair decision because corrosion at the seam or base cannot be corrected with a new valve or heating element. We use the serial number and visible condition of the jacket, fittings, and drain area to separate a serviceable component fault from a tank that has reached the end of its useful condition.

Access also affects the work. A heater in an open garage allows a different repair path than a unit in a tight closet, attic platform, or finished utility room with drywall, shelves, and a narrow drain pan around it.

A shutoff valve that will not turn, a corroded supply connector, or a relief valve discharge line that needs correction can add work beyond the original failed part. Special-order controls, uncommon burner parts, and any required sign-off can also move the final scope because they change the materials, return visit, or installation steps.

sections.heading: Model number and tank location
paragraphs: Before calling, find the model and serial number on the rating plate attached to the water heater jacket. Tell us whether the unit sits in a garage, closet, attic, utility room, or another space, and whether a door, stairs, or stored items restrict access.

Note whether water is running from the relief pipe, drain valve, top connections, or the bottom of the tank. If the heater still produces some hot water, mention whether the water turns cold after a few minutes or stays cold at every faucet.

For a gas unit, let us know whether the pilot or burner is lit; for an electric unit, note any tripped breaker or reset button. Call JPT Cedar Park Plumbing at (512) 818-1571 before an active tank leak spreads into the floor, wall, or ceiling below.

services.name: Toilet Repair
services.h1: Toilet Repair in Cedar Park, TX
services.title: Toilet Repair | JPT Cedar Park Plumbing | Cedar Park, TX, TX
services.meta: JPT Cedar Park Plumbing provides toilet repair in Cedar Park, TX, TX for running tanks, weak flushes, base leaks, and failed fill valves at home.
services.blurb: We inspect running tanks, weak flushes, leaks at the base, and worn toilet parts.

paragraphs: A tank that refills every few minutes can seem minor at first, but a week of running water sends more water through the fill valve and overflow tube than most homeowners expect. Over a month, a worn flapper can keep cycling, a weak fill valve can grow louder, and mineral buildup can slow the refill even further. We check the tank parts before a small refill problem turns into a toilet that will not flush.

Water around the toilet base changes the priority because the wax ring, closet bolts, or bowl can allow water beneath the flooring. A loose bowl can work against the flange with every use, while a slow leak can stain vinyl, swell wood, or dampen the subfloor. A quiet refill may wait for a planned repair if the floor stays dry, but base leaks, overflow, and a toilet that will not flush should not wait because water and waste can reach the floor.

sections.heading: Running tank and weak flush
paragraphs: Customers often call us because the toilet keeps running after a flush, the bowl barely clears paper, or the handle has to be held down to finish the flush. Other calls start with water appearing at the base, a tank that fills slowly, a hissing sound behind the lid, or a bowl water level that drops between uses. A failed flapper, worn fill valve, sticking trip lever, damaged flush valve seal, loose tank bolt, or leaking wax ring can produce symptoms that seem similar from outside the fixture. Those faults require different parts and different labor, so an inspection separates a simple tank repair from work involving the bowl, flange, or flooring.

sections.heading: Tank and bowl inspection
paragraphs: We begin at the tank by operating the handle, watching the chain and flapper seat, and checking the water line against the overflow tube. A dye test can expose a flapper leak in about fifteen to thirty minutes, and we measure the flush valve opening because many tanks use either a two-inch or three-inch valve. If the fill valve hisses, chatters, or fills slowly, we inspect the angle stop, supply connector, and incoming pressure with a gauge; residential supply pressure commonly falls within a forty-to-eighty-psi range. We can usually replace a flapper, fill valve, trip lever, supply connector, or tank seal during the visit, while a cracked bowl, damaged flange, specialty tank part, or floor repair may require parts ordering or a separate booking.

sections.heading: Shutoff valves and flange access
paragraphs: The age of the tank hardware affects the repair scope because older toilets may use a flush valve seal, handle, or fill valve that does not match common replacement parts. A seized angle stop can add work before we can disconnect the supply line, especially where corrosion has locked the valve stem or compression nut. Access at the base also matters: rusted closet bolts, tile around the bowl, a loose flange, or soft flooring can require the toilet to come up before we can reach the failed seal. A tank-specific part that must be ordered, or a floor and drain alteration that needs inspection sign-off, adds steps beyond a standard flapper or fill valve replacement.

sections.heading: Tank model and flush valve
paragraphs: We ask for the model number printed inside the tank or stamped on the underside of the lid when that marking is available. We also need to know which bathroom holds the toilet and whether the fixture is a standard tank toilet, a pressure-assisted unit, or a wall-hung bowl. A photo of the tank interior, flush valve opening, and water at the base can help us identify likely parts before we arrive. We ask whether the toilet is running now, whether the floor feels soft, and whether cabinets or flooring restrict access to the angle stop. Call JPT Cedar Park Plumbing at (512) 818-1571 if water remains at the base, because a leaking wax ring can continue soaking the flooring and subfloor.

services.name: Pipe Leak Repair
services.h1: Pipe Leak Repair in Cedar Park, TX
services.title: Pipe Leak Repair | JPT Cedar Park Plumbing | Cedar Park, TX, TX
services.meta: JPT Cedar Park Plumbing finds and repairs leaking pipe, joints, and fittings in Cedar Park, TX, TX, Anderson Mill, Brushy Creek, and Jollyville.
services.blurb: We trace leaking pipes, isolate the water, and repair damaged joints and fittings.

paragraphs: A towel beneath a cabinet, a bowl under a drip, and a closed fixture shutoff are sensible first steps when water appears where it should not. They catch water and can limit damage to a cabinet floor, baseboard, or countertop while you look for the source. But a towel cannot stop water moving through a pinhole, a loose fitting, or a split section of pipe behind the wall.

Water can travel along framing, insulation, and drywall before it makes a visible stain on a ceiling or wall. A small drip inside a cabinet can also swell particleboard, damage flooring, and create a mildew odor. Pipe leak repair should not wait because water keeps reaching building materials even after the visible puddle has been wiped up.

sections.heading: Water stains and hissing
paragraphs: People call us about a brown ring spreading across a ceiling, a hissing sound behind a bathroom wall, or a damp patch under a kitchen sink that returns after drying. Others notice a cabinet floor that stays wet, peeling paint near a baseboard, or a water meter that keeps moving while every faucet remains off. A warm spot on a slab floor can point to a hot-water line, while a musty odor from a closet may come from moisture trapped behind drywall. A pinhole in copper pipe, a failed fitting, and a leaking valve connection can look much alike at first, but each fault requires different materials, access work, and labor.

sections.heading: Leak inspection
paragraphs: We start a leak inspection by locating the wet area, checking exposed pipe and fittings, and asking where water first appeared. We read the water meter, check fixture shutoffs, and measure static water pressure; residential supply pressure commonly falls between 40 and 80 psi. A first inspection often takes 30 to 60 minutes, depending on whether the pipe runs through a cabinet, crawlspace, wall, ceiling, or slab.

For an exposed copper, PEX, or CPVC line, we can often isolate the water, remove the damaged section, and install new pipe and fittings on the same visit. We check common 1/2-inch and 3/4-inch branch lines for corrosion, rubbing, loose supports, and failed joints before restoring water. A leak behind tile, under a slab, or inside a finished wall may need a return visit after access is opened, replacement pipe is obtained, or the repair area can be reached without damaging more drywall.

sections.heading: Shutoffs, walls, and pipe
paragraphs: Pipe material, wall access, and the condition of nearby shutoff valves all change the scope of a repair. An exposed copper elbow under a sink usually takes less access work than a damaged pipe behind tile, cabinetry, concrete, or ceiling drywall. If a corroded shutoff will not close, we may need to isolate water farther back on the line before the damaged fitting can be removed.

Older galvanized pipe can shed rust inside the line, and a repair may reveal that adjacent threaded sections need attention as well. A specialty fitting or matching section of pipe may need to be ordered if the existing material or connection does not match standard stock. Work that requires wall restoration, property approval, or municipal sign-off adds separate steps beyond repairing the leaking pipe itself.

sections.heading: Pipe material and wall access
paragraphs: Before calling, note which room has the leak, whether it is under a sink, above a ceiling, behind a wall, or near an appliance water connection. If pipe is visible, a clear photo can show whether it is copper, PEX, CPVC, or galvanized steel and whether a shutoff valve sits nearby. Tell us if water continues to run with the fixture shutoff closed, or if the water meter moves after faucets and appliances have been turned off.

Let us know whether a cabinet, crawlspace hatch, attic opening, or removable drywall panel provides access to the pipe. If the leak sits near a dishwasher, refrigerator, or washing machine connection, the appliance model label can help identify the supply setup. Call JPT Cedar Park Plumbing at (512) 818-1571 before water reaches more framing, insulation, ceiling drywall, or flooring.

services.name: Faucet Repair
services.h1: Faucet Repair in Cedar Park, TX
services.title: Faucets | JPT Cedar Park Plumbing | Cedar Park, TX, TX
services.meta: JPT Cedar Park Plumbing repairs dripping, loose, leaking, and low-flow faucets in Cedar Park, TX, TX. Call (512) 818-1571 with the faucet model.
services.blurb: We repair dripping, leaking, loose, and low-flow faucets in Cedar Park.

paragraphs: Homeowners call us when “the faucet won’t stop dripping,” “the handle just spins,” or “water is coming out around the base.” Those words point us toward the parts inside the faucet: a worn cartridge, a loose handle screw, a damaged O-ring, or a supply connection beneath the sink. We start with what the faucet does at the spout, handle, and base rather than assuming every leak has the same source.

A kitchen faucet may leave a small puddle beside the sink after the handle shuts off, while a bathroom faucet may run a narrow stream all day. A pull-down sprayer can leak from the hose connection, and a two-handle faucet can drip because one stem no longer closes against its seat. We check the fixture, the shutoff valves, and the cabinet floor to locate the water path.

A slow drip can often wait for a planned repair if the shutoff valves work and the cabinet stays dry. Water beneath the sink, a handle that will not turn off, or a faucet spraying from its body should not wait, because water can soak the cabinet, flooring, supply lines, and wall behind the fixture.

sections.heading: Drip and loose handle
paragraphs: “My faucet keeps dripping” can mean water escapes from the spout after the handle closes, but it can also mean water works out around the handle cap or gathers at the faucet base. “The handle is loose” may describe a missing set screw, a worn handle adapter, or a cartridge stem that no longer holds the handle in position. Each fault changes how we access and repair the fixture.

Customers also report “barely any water comes out,” “the sprayer leaks under the sink,” and “the faucet makes a squeal.” Low flow often starts at a clogged aerator or screen, while a squeal can come from a restricted cartridge, loose washer, or pressure change through the valve. A leak at the pull-down hose can show only when the sprayer extends from its dock.

These symptoms can look alike from the countertop, especially when water runs down the faucet body and into the sink. Once we remove the handle, inspect the cartridge, and check the hose and supply connections, we can separate a small replaceable part from a faucet body or valve problem; the required parts and labor depend on that finding.

sections.heading: Cartridge inspection at the sink
paragraphs: At the fixture, we run hot and cold water, watch the spout and base, and inspect the handle travel. We check the aerator for mineral buildup, look under the sink for moisture at the supply tubes and shutoff valves, and identify the faucet make from the plate or body. A basic faucet inspection commonly takes 15 to 30 minutes when the cabinet and fixture are accessible.

Before removing a cartridge or stem, we close the hot and cold shutoff valves and confirm that they stop water at the faucet. We then remove the handle, cap, retaining nut, and cartridge or stem as the fixture design requires. A worn O-ring, seal, aerator, handle screw, or standard cartridge can often be replaced during the same visit if the matching part is available.

We test the faucet after reassembly by operating both sides of the handle, checking the spout, base, spray hose, and cabinet connections for water. A corroded valve body, seized shutoff, discontinued cartridge, or faucet that needs replacement may require a return visit after the correct part or fixture is obtained.

sections.heading: Cartridge age and shutoff valve
paragraphs: The age and design of the cartridge affect the repair. A common single-handle cartridge may come out after the retaining clip is removed, while an older stem can have corrosion at the bonnet nut, seat, or threads. Faucet brands also use different splines, stem lengths, seals, and retaining hardware, so a close-looking replacement does not always fit.

Cabinet access changes the work beneath the sink. Cleaning supplies, a disposal, drawer hardware, or a tight vanity can limit access to shutoff valves and supply connections. A shutoff valve that has seized or leaks when operated adds work because we need to address the valve before safely opening the faucet.

A special-order cartridge, discontinued handle, or matching finish part can move the repair beyond a standard visit. In a rental, condominium, or commercial restroom, owner approval or building sign-off can also add coordination before a fixture or valve is changed.

sections.heading: Model number and faucet plate
paragraphs: Before calling, check which room contains the faucet and whether it serves a kitchen sink, bathroom sink, laundry sink, bar sink, or tub. Look for a brand mark on the handle cap, escutcheon plate, spout, or spray head; some model numbers appear on a label beneath the sink or on the original installation paperwork.

Note whether the faucet has one handle, two handles, a side sprayer, or a pull-down hose. Tell us whether water drips from the spout, escapes around the handle, leaks under the cabinet, or runs only while the sprayer is pulled out.

If you know the approximate age of the faucet, share that along with any previous cartridge or handle repair. Clear the cabinet enough to reach the shutoff valves, and let us know if either valve appears stuck or if water is running now.

Call JPT Cedar Park Plumbing at (512) 818-1571 with the faucet model or brand mark. A drip at the spout can become cabinet damage when the leak shifts to the base, hose, or supply connection and continues beneath the sink.

services.name: Garbage Disposal Repair
services.h1: Garbage Disposal Repair in Cedar Park, TX
services.title: Garbage Disposal Repair | JPT Cedar Park Plumbing | Cedar Park, TX, TX
services.meta: JPT Cedar Park Plumbing repairs jammed, humming, leaking, and clogged garbage disposals in Cedar Park, TX, TX, Anderson Mill, Brushy Creek, and Jollyville.
services.blurb: We repair humming, jammed, leaking, and clogged garbage disposals in Cedar Park.

paragraphs: Older homes around Cedar Park, Anderson Mill, Brushy Creek, and Jollyville often have a disposal that has worked through years of food scraps, detergent, and hard-water residue. The grinding chamber, splash guard, mounting ring, and drain connection all wear differently, so a sink that once cleared quickly can begin holding water or making a low hum. We check the unit beneath the kitchen sink rather than assuming a slow bowl points to one failed part.

A disposal commonly lasts about 8 to 15 years, though a utensil in the chamber, swollen food waste, or a loose wire can stop a newer unit as well. We look at the reset button, breaker, switch, sink flange, and discharge tube to trace the fault. A humming motor, backed-up sink, or water under the cabinet should not wait, because a stalled motor can overheat and standing water can damage the cabinet floor and drain connections.

sections.heading: Humming motor and sink odor
paragraphs: We hear several distinct descriptions on disposal calls: “it hums but will not spin,” “the sink fills when the dishwasher drains,” “water is leaking under the cabinet,” and “the kitchen sink smells rotten.” A hum often means the flywheel cannot turn, while a silent unit can point to the reset button, wall switch, breaker, or wiring connection. Water around the disposal can come from the sink flange, dishwasher inlet, discharge elbow, mounting assembly, or the disposal housing itself. A sour odor may come from food caught beneath the splash guard or residue sitting in the grinding chamber. These symptoms can sound alike from the kitchen counter, but each one leads to a different repair path and different parts once we inspect the motor and drain connection.

sections.heading: Under-sink callout testing
paragraphs: We start the callout by checking the cabinet for moisture, running the faucet, and testing the wall switch, breaker, and reset button. With power isolated, we inspect the grinding chamber for glass, bone fragments, cutlery, and packed food, then turn the flywheel with the proper disposal wrench where the unit allows it. We also run water through the sink and dishwasher connection, watching the discharge tube and trap for a backup or leak. A simple obstruction, reset, loose connection, splash guard, or drain fitting can often be handled during a 30- to 60-minute visit. A cracked housing, failed motor, seized mounting ring, or replacement unit that needs a specific model may require a return visit after the correct part or disposal arrives.

sections.heading: Mounting ring and shutoff valve
paragraphs: The disposal’s age affects the repair because older motors, sink flanges, and mounting assemblies may no longer match current replacement parts. Cabinet access also changes the work: a deep sink, tight corner cabinet, fixed shelving, or crowded water lines can limit room for the wrench, bucket, and drain tools. A seized shutoff valve or brittle supply line near the cabinet can add work if it must be moved or replaced to reach the disposal connection safely. We also check whether the existing electrical cord, dishwasher inlet, and drain outlet line up with a replacement model. A standard-size unit with open access and an available part usually involves less work than a cracked unit, corroded fittings, or a model that must be ordered.

sections.heading: Model plate and sink cabinet
paragraphs: Before calling, we ask customers to look for the model number on the disposal’s label or model plate, usually on the side or bottom of the unit beneath the sink. The make and model help us identify the mounting style, horsepower class, reset location, and compatible parts. Let us know which kitchen sink bowl has the disposal, whether the dishwasher connects to it, and whether the unit hums, leaks, or trips the breaker when switched on. A clear photo of the cabinet, drain pipe, and mounting ring can also show whether shelves, cleaning products, or water lines restrict access. Please tell us if water is standing in the sink or collecting on the cabinet floor when you call JPT Cedar Park Plumbing at (512) 818-1571. A leak at the disposal or discharge tube can keep soaking the cabinet base and nearby wood if the repair waits.
